title: AI CEOs are in their manifesto era
excerpt: AI CEOs keep publishing lengthy missives. While unlikely to be read beyond techies, the CEOs want to "own" the narrative, communications advisers say.
content_html:
By Henry Chandonnet

You're currently following this author! Want to unfollow? Unsubscribe via the link in your email.

Mark Zuckerberg is often sparing with his words. On Monday, he published over 6,000 of them.

Executives from the leading AI companies keep writing long, long manifestos. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei is the biggest player in lengthy essay-writing. His "Machines of Loving Grace" — which clocks in at over 13,000 words — has been printed, bound, and given out as merch.

Meanwhile, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella has taken to posting long essays this year about the AI economy, and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman writes blog posts about the future. Maybe the only abstainer is Elon Musk, who seems to prefer shorter posts and replies on X.

The CEOs' trend toward wordiness is a bit ironic. Americans are reading less for pleasure, while social video platforms like TikTok soar. AI could be accelerating this change; one wonders how many people have asked Claude for a quick summary of an Amodei essay.

It's unlikely that much of the American public is sitting down with thousands of words from an AI CEO. So, what's the point?

"They become these long treatises that you're nailing to the church door," said Patrick Riccards, a strategic communications advisor and CEO of Driving Force Institute. "The heft of their message carries a gravitas."

In AI, writing is all the rage

Zuckerberg's essay charted a "path to a positive AI future." It's a common trope for these companies' leaders: prophesying how AI will rise.

Amodei's classic 2024 essay has a similar subtitle: "How AI could transform the world for the better." While Zuckerberg narrows in on the economy and government, Amodei spends more time with biology and neuroscience. The essay has since been printed as a book and resold on eBay.

Nadella and Demis Hassabis, Google DeepMind's former CEO who recently announced his transition to chair of the AI lab, use their X essays to ask big questions. In his much-praised post, Hassabis proposed a self-regulatory "Standards Body."

Then there's Altman, who seems to have backed off his philosophical blogging. He once wrote long posts about the singularity and AI economics; now, his posts are often product updates or reflections on his family's life.

While Altman has slowed his own lengthier writing, he has criticized the words of his rivals. He used one blog to link a critical story in The New Yorker to a Molotov cocktail attack on his home.

"Words have power," Altman wrote. "I am awake in the middle of the night and pissed, and thinking that I have underestimated the power of words and narratives."

What's with the writing craze? Riccards said that it was about creating an ideological paper trail, one that the CEOs can cite down the line. He also pointed to control: "You own every word of it."

Melissa Swift, founder of the organizational consulting firm Anthrome Insight, said that these CEOs have "very pure" impulses: they want to be understood. But that's not always the effect, she said.

"The longer a document you put on the page with your unfiltered thoughts, the more likely it is to be misunderstood," she said.

Is anyone reading these essays?

Attention spans are fracturing, and many Americans are more inclined to scroll Reels than pick up a book. (Zuckerberg should know this, as he also runs Instagram.) So, does anyone actually read these manifestos?

Riccards gave a quick "no." Maybe they're read by the labs' competitors or the venture capitalists, he said. "I'm surprised you don't see more of these CEOs doing this as a video," he said.

Swift pushed back against the video impulse, saying that they often look "heavily edited" or "like a hostage video."

She gave two readership demographics: the media (you're welcome!), and the tech superfans. The problem, Swift said, was that the superfans were within the same "Silicon Valley echo chamber" as the CEOs.

"The superfans are clapping with each one, but the rest of the country — both geographically and by each industry — have a different reaction," she said.

作者：Henry Chandonnet 您目前正在关注该作者！ 想要取消关注吗？ 通过电子邮件中的链接取消订阅。

马克·扎克伯格经常少言寡语。 周一，他发表了 6,000 多篇文章。

领先的人工智能公司的高管们一直在写很长很长的宣言。 Anthropic 首席执行官达里奥·阿莫迪 (Dario Amodei) 是长篇论文写作领域的最大参与者。 他的《爱的机器》——总计超过 13,000 字——已被印刷、装订并作为商品分发。

与此同时，微软首席执行官萨蒂亚·纳德拉（Satya Nadella）今年开始发表有关人工智能经济的长篇文章，OpenAI 首席执行官萨姆·奥尔特曼（Sam Altman）撰写了有关未来的博客文章。 也许唯一的弃权者是埃隆·马斯克（Elon Musk），他似乎更喜欢 X 上较短的帖子和回复。

CEO们的啰嗦倾向有点讽刺。 美国人为了消遣而阅读的内容越来越少，而 TikTok 等社交视频平台却在飙升。 人工智能可能会加速这一变化；人们想知道有多少人向克劳德询问阿莫代论文的快速摘要。

大多数美国公众不太可能坐下来听人工智能首席执行官的数千句话。 那么，有什么意义呢？

“它们变成了钉在教堂门上的长篇论文，”驱动力研究所战略传播顾问兼首席执行官帕特里克·里卡兹 (Patrick Riccards) 说。 “他们传达的信息充满庄重感。”

在人工智能领域，写作风靡一时

扎克伯格的文章描绘了一条“通往积极的人工智能未来之路”。 这些公司的领导者有一个共同的比喻：预言人工智能将如何崛起。

Amodei 在 2024 年发表的经典文章也有类似的副标题：“人工智能如何让世界变得更美好”。 扎克伯格的关注范围缩小到经济和政府，而阿莫迪则将更多时间花在生物学和神经科学上。 这篇文章已被印刷成书并在 eBay 上转售。

纳德拉 (Nadella) 和谷歌 DeepMind 前首席执行官德米斯·哈萨比斯 (Demis Hassabis) 最近宣布转任人工智能实验室主席，他们利用他们的 X 论文提出了重大问题。 哈萨比斯在他广受好评的帖子中提出了一个自我监管的“标准机构”。

然后是奥特曼，他似乎已经放弃了他的哲学博客。 他曾经写过关于奇点和人工智能经济学的长篇文章；现在，他的帖子通常是产品更新或对家庭生活的反思。

虽然奥特曼放慢了自己较长的写作速度，但他批评了竞争对手的言论。 他利用一个博客将《纽约客》上的一篇评论文章与他家遭受的燃烧弹袭击联系起来。

“言语具有力量，”奥特曼写道。 “我半夜醒来，很生气，我想我低估了文字和叙述的力量。”

写作热潮是怎么回事？ 里卡兹表示，这是为了创建一份意识形态文件记录，首席执行官们可以随时引用。 他还指着控制：“你拥有它的每一个字。”

组织咨询公司Anthrome Insight的创始人梅丽莎·斯威夫特(Melissa Swift)表示，这些CEO有“非常纯粹”的冲动：他们希望被理解。 但她说，效果并不总是如此。

“你在页面上放置未经过滤的想法的文件越长，它就越有可能被误解，”她说。

有人读这些文章吗？

注意力分散，许多美国人更倾向于滚动卷轴而不是拿起一本书。 （扎克伯格应该知道这一点，因为他也运营着 Instagram。） 那么，有人真正读过这些宣言吗？

里卡兹很快就说“不”。 他说，也许实验室的竞争对手或风险投资家会阅读它们。 “我很惊讶你没有看到更多的首席执行官通过视频来做到这一点，”他说。

斯威夫特抵制了视频冲动，称它们通常看起来“经过大量编辑”或“像人质视频”。

她提供了两种读者群统计数据：媒体（不客气！）和科技超级粉丝。 斯威夫特说，问题在于超级粉丝与首席执行官们处于同一个“硅谷回音室”。

“超级粉丝们都在为每个人鼓掌，但全国其他地区——无论是在地理上还是在每个行业——都有不同的反应，”她说。
